title: KV memory tiering, DRAM and SSD
summary: The spiral's evicted context given somewhere to go: a cluster DRAM pool a quarter the size of what it would swap, an SSD pool under it at a single drive's bandwidth, and then one shared fabric that every migration has to cross.

steps.title: The same spiral: parked context fills HBM at two sessions a second
body: Four replicas with a 30,000-token cache each, chat sessions of eight turns with eight seconds of thinking between them. Every parked session holds its whole context between turns, and the cache is full inside a minute at an offered load the devices could serve fifty times over. This is finding 8's kv-spiral, with the swap path kept.

What changes here is where the evicted context goes. In kv-spiral-swap each replica had four caches' worth of host DRAM to itself and parked up to 111,000 tokens fleet-wide at its peak. This run, tier-dram, gives the fleet one cluster DRAM pool of 28,000 tokens, about a quarter of that, and nothing under it.
steps.look_for: KV utilization at the cap on every replica while queue depth stays near zero; the preemption rate settling at about 2.3 a second, the same as the swap run's 2.2.

steps.title: A quarter-sized DRAM pool absorbs it, and what overflows is recomputed
body: The pool fills: DRAM utilization (tier 1 of METRIC_TIER_UTILIZATION on the fleet row) runs at 43% on average and touches 99.8% at its peak. A victim that finds it full is dropped and pays its prefill again when its turn comes, chunked at 1,024 tokens a step like any other prompt.

That is three quarters of the cure taken away, and the run does not mind: 1,421 tokens/s of goodput at 100% attainment, against kv-spiral-swap's 1,376 at 97.6%. The overflow costs time to first token, p99 233 ms against 84 ms, because a returning turn waits for its recompute. It buys inter-token latency, p99 70 ms against 82 ms, because a synchronous 26 ms copy no longer lands in every decoding sequence's gap. Under an 80 ms ITL objective that trade is a win.
steps.look_for: Preemptions continuing at 2.3 a second with attainment at 100%; the DRAM path busy for 2% of each window on average, never above 23%.

steps.title: An SSD pool under it, at a single drive's 10 GB/s: five times the transfer, and worse than dropping
body: tier-dram-ssd adds a 120,000-token cluster SSD pool, large enough for everything the swap run ever parked, at 10 GB/s: one Gen5 drive rather than the 50 GB/s of eight striped, which section 7.2 gives as the default. Nothing is dropped any more. SSD fills to 14% on average and 58% at peak, and its path is busy 13% of the time, saturated for whole windows at the worst moments.

Every one of those transfers takes five times as long as the DRAM copy it replaced, 131 ms for a 4,000-token context, and it is charged to the step that made it. Throughput holds at 1,411 tokens/s, so the tier is doing its job as capacity. Goodput falls to 893 and attainment to 70.3%: ITL p99 is 361 ms, TTFT p99 323 ms. In the last third of the run only 42% of requests meet every objective. A tier slower than the ITL budget is worse than no tier.
steps.look_for: Throughput flat while goodput drops by a third; ITL p99 four and a half times the objective.

steps.title: One 10 GB/s fabric shared by every migration: swap becomes a queue
body: Open the A/B view with A = tier-dram (this run) and B = tier-contended: the same pools behind one shared fabric of 10 GB/s. A migration now starts when the fabric is free and its wall time, queueing included, is what the step is charged. METRIC_TIER_BANDWIDTH_UTILIZATION reads 22% busy on average and pinned at 100% in 12% of all windows, which is the queue forming.

Goodput 666 tokens/s at 59.6% attainment, TTFT p99 4.2 s, ITL p99 2.4 s, 15% of late requests within objective. Throughput drops to 1,174 because the devices spend their time waiting for copies. Preemptions rise to 2.4 a second. This is section 7.2's "until the shared bandwidth saturates": at 666 the swap advantage has inverted, barely above the 608 of the run that never swaps at all.
steps.look_for: A and B separating on every headline: attainment 100% against 59.6%, TTFT p99 233 ms against 4.2 s, with the same offered load and the same preemption rate.

steps.title: A tier is a cure only when its transfer fits the ITL budget and its fabric is not shared with the migrations it creates
body: Three rungs, one workload: a quarter-sized DRAM pool serves the spiral at 100% attainment and 1,421 tokens/s; a single-drive SSD tier that catches every overflow drops attainment to 70.3%; a 10 GB/s fabric shared by every migration drops it to 59.6% and turns swap into a queue.

The sizing question is not how much tier capacity to buy. Dropping three quarters of the victims and recomputing them cost nothing that mattered. It is whether a migration's transfer time, queueing included, stays under the inter-token objective, because that is where a synchronous copy lands.
steps.look_for: DRAM utilization still peaking near 100% in this run while attainment holds at 100%: the pool is small and full, and that is fine.
